terms.gloss: youth, the years between boyhood and manhood
evidence: Cic. Sen. 70: vēr enim tamquam adulēscentiam significat
terms.comment: The age of the adulēscēns, which Lewis & Short put roughly from fifteen to thirty: after pueritia (see childhood) and before juventūs in the strict sense. The everyday word for one’s youth.

terms.register: vōx plērumque poētica et post Augustum: Verg., Ov.; Liv.
terms.comment: Mostly post-Augustan for the classical juventūs (Lewis & Short).

terms.gloss: the age of youth (strictly from twenty to forty)
evidence: Sall. C. 5.2: ibique juventūtem suam exercuit (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: In this sense rare; far more often young people collectively (see youth, young people) (Lewis & Short).

phrases.latin: vēr enim tamquam adulēscentiam significat ostenditque frūctūs futūrōs
phrases.english: for spring stands for youth, as it were, and shows the fruit to come

phrases.latin: frūctuōsior est adulēscentia līberōrum, sed īnfantia dulcior
phrases.english: children’s youth bears more fruit, but their infancy is sweeter

phrases.latin: in hujus sinū indulgentiāque ēducātus per omnem honestārum artium cultum pueritiam adulēscentiamque trānsēgit
phrases.english: brought up in her lap and her loving care, he spent his childhood and youth in the study of every honourable art

sources: Lewis & Short: adulescentia · Lewis & Short: juventa · Lewis & Short: juventus
John C. Traupman, Conversational Latin for Oral Proficiency, p. 78: “youth (age) adulēscentia”.
